query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy, the alternating soft and hard phases develop dissimilar oxide films at elevated temperature. Under simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive attack, the mechanically induced spallation of a poorly adherent and phase‐specific oxide film exposes a chemically active substrate that promotes micro‐galvanic corrosion at the phase interfaces. This cyclic oxide disruption and reformation accelerates both wear and localized corrosion in a mutually reinforcing (synergistic) degradation process.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy with a lamellar microstructure comprising alternating phases (for example a soft FCC phase and a hard BCC phase as seen in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 systems).
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to simultaneous sliding wear and corrosive attack at an elevated temperature (e.g., ~600–800 °C) rather than under inert or individually isolated wear/corrosion conditions.
generation.conditions: Testing in a corrosive environment (such as chloride-containing sulfuric acid or similar aggressive electrolyte) at elevated temperature where oxide growth is rapid and adhesion is poor, combined with cyclic mechanical wear (sliding or reciprocating) that removes surface oxides.
generation.structural_mediator: Phase-dependent, non-uniform oxide films that form differently on the soft and hard phases create local galvanic cells at phase boundaries; these, combined with microstructural heterogeneities inherent to the eutectic lamellar structure, act as mediators of the synergistic degradation.
generation.mechanism: At high temperature, each phase forms its own oxide layer with differing adhesion and protectiveness. Mechanical wear cyclically removes the protective oxide from the more corrosion‐sensitive phase, thereby exposing a fresh reactive surface. The differential corrosion kinetics between adjacent phases then induce micro-galvanic effects that further weaken the oxide integrity and substrate. This positive feedback cycle leads to accelerated total degradation as both wear and corrosion intensify in tandem.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a matched baseline (e.g., the same alloy subjected to wear alone in an inert environment or corrosion alone without mechanical disruption), the alloy will exhibit a higher overall degradation rate. Specifically, the total material loss (combined wear and corrosion volume loss) will be significantly higher, while the corrosion damage (e.g., higher corrosion current density and deeper pitting) and wear damage (e.g., increased wear track volume loss) will each be exacerbated due to the synergistic interaction.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the same eutectic HEA tested under isolated conditions: (a) purely mechanical wear in an inert environment at elevated temperature, and (b) corrosion in the absence of mechanical wear, where a continuous, more protective oxide layer can form.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate under sufficiently high temperatures (e.g., 600–800 °C) and in corrosive media that can promote non-uniform, poorly adherent oxide films. These conditions must be met for the micro-galvanic coupling and cyclic oxide removal to become significant; in inert or room-temperature environments, or in truly uniform single-phase alloys, the effect is expected to be minimal or absent.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contribution of the oxide spallation versus inherent galvanic effects in accelerating degradation is uncertain, as is the exact magnitude of the synergistic increase in material loss; further experiments are required to decouple and quantify these contributions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens of the same multi-phase eutectic HEA. One set is tested under simultaneous sliding wear in a corrosive environment at elevated temperature, while the control set is subjected to identical elevated-temperature corrosion conditions but with minimal mechanical wear (e.g., by using a static immersion test or very low friction conditions). Alternatively, one could test the alloy under wear in a non-aggressive, inert atmosphere. Compare the degradation rates (wear volume loss, corrosion current, pitting depth) between the two sets.
measurements: Wear track volume loss via profilometry or microscopy
Electrochemical measurements (potentiodynamic polarization curves, corrosion current density)
Surface composition and oxide scale integrity by XPS or SEM/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimens under simultaneous wear and corrosion at high temperature do not show statistically significant higher total degradation or if the individual indicators of accelerated wear and corrosion (compared to the respective baselines) are not observed, then the hypothesis that cyclic oxide spallation and micro-galvanic corrosion drive the accelerated coupled degradation is falsified.

Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding

Abstract: To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2).
